summary: An update to the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, revising earlier notes (RFC 10 and RFC 16) about how the group's notes are written and distributed. Later revisions followed in RFC 27 and RFC 30.

eli5.summary: This note updates the group's rules about how to write and share notes, because the first set needed some changes.

questions: what were the nwg documentation conventions
subtitle: The 1969 ground rules for writing and circulating Network Working Group notes.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group wanted people to exchange ideas freely, but unpolished thoughts are hard to publish when written statements are taken as authoritative.
tldr.mechanism: Notes may contain any thought related to HOST software or the network, must carry a standard header, and are mailed in one copy to a list of eleven people.
tldr.outcome: It revises RFC 10 and RFC 16 and was itself updated by later RFCs.

today: The metadata lists no obsoleting RFC, but RFC 24 was updated by RFC 27 and RFC 30. It revised RFC 10 and RFC 16.

sections.title: The Working Group and Its Notes
sections.content:
This note revises NWG/RFC 10 and 16. The Network Working Group (NWG) consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites, and membership is not closed. The group is concerned with HOST software, strategies for using the network, and initial experience with the network.

Its work is documented through notes like this one, which may be produced at any site and included in the series.
sections.eli5: The group is an open club of people who care about getting computers to talk, and they share their thoughts as notes.

sections.title: Content
sections.content:
A note may be any thought or suggestion related to HOST software or another aspect of the network. Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples, suggestions without background, and questions without attempted answers are all acceptable. The minimum length is one sentence.

The text gives two reasons. People tend to treat any written statement as authoritative, and the group hopes to promote discussion of far less authoritative ideas. There is also a natural hesitancy to publish something unpolished, which the group wants to ease.
sections.eli5: Your note does not have to be perfect or long. One sentence is enough, so nobody is afraid to share.

sections.title: Form
sections.content: Every note should carry four things: the heading "Network Working Group" and "Request for Comments: X" where X is a serial number assigned by Steve Crocker at UCLA, the author and affiliation, the date, and a title. The title need not be unique.
sections.eli5: Every note gets a number, a name, a date and a title, like the label on a homework paper.

sections.title: Distribution and Addresses
sections.content:
The author's site sends one copy only to each of eleven named people at MIT, Utah, SDC, UCLA, SRI, MITRE, RAND, BB&N, ARPA and Lincoln Laboratory. Reproduction, if desired, may be handled locally.

The note ends with a list of the most current postal addresses and phone numbers the author had, and asks readers to correct them as necessary.
sections.eli5: You mail one copy to each person on the list, and they can make more copies themselves if they want.
